title: The Great Train Robbery: What Really Happened

beats.say: In the early hours of the eighth of August nineteen sixty three, a gang stopped a Royal Mail train in the Buckinghamshire countryside with a glove and a battery. Fifteen minutes later, they had two point six million pounds.

vis.text: A glove, a battery, and £2.6 million.

beats.say: That's around forty eight million pounds in today's money. It became known as the Great Train Robbery, and some of the men who did it became household names.
But the legend leaves out a lot. A train driver who was badly hurt. A hideout full of fingerprints. And a famous game of Monopoly that helped send the gang to prison.
Part one. The mail train.
Every night, a travelling post office train ran from Glasgow to London. In one carriage, called the high value packages coach, it carried used banknotes being sent back to London to be destroyed.
After a bank holiday weekend, there was even more cash on board than usual. The gang had been tipped off. They knew exactly which coach to target, and roughly how much would be inside.

vis.text: They knew which coach. And how much.

beats.say: The gang was large, around fifteen men, and many had criminal records. Some were experienced robbers from south London. They planned for months, studying the route, the timings, and the quiet stretch of railway where they'd strike.

vis.title: The planning
items: Chose a quiet stretch of line

beats.say: They even brought along someone they thought could drive the train, so they could move it to the bridge where their lorries were waiting. But on the night, he couldn't operate it, so they forced Jack Mills to drive instead.

vis.text: Their 'train driver' couldn't drive the train.

beats.say: Part two. The fake red light.
At Sears Crossing in Buckinghamshire, the gang tampered with a railway signal. They covered the green light with a glove, and used a battery to light up the red one.
The driver, Jack Mills, did exactly what he was trained to do. He stopped. When his co-driver climbed down to phone the signal box, he found the line had been cut.

events: Train stops at the red light

beats.say: Then the gang attacked. Jack Mills was hit over the head and badly injured. He never fully recovered from what happened that night.

vis.text: Train driver injured as gang raids mail train
vis.date: Jack Mills never fully recovered from the attack

beats.say: The robbers forced the train forward to Bridego Bridge, where their vehicles were waiting. They formed a human chain and passed down more than a hundred mail bags. The whole thing took around fifteen minutes.

vis.label: to empty the high value coach

beats.say: Part three. The farm.
The gang drove to Leatherslade Farm, a run-down farmhouse around twenty seven miles away, which they'd bought as a hideout. There they counted the money and shared it out.
While they waited for things to calm down, some of them played Monopoly. With the real money, according to some versions of the story.
But they left the farm in a hurry when they heard police were searching the area. And the plan to clean the place up, or burn it down, never happened properly.
Part four. The fingerprints.

On the thirteenth of August, police found Leatherslade Farm. Inside were empty mail bags, food, vehicles, and that Monopoly board. Fingerprints on the board, on a sauce bottle and on other items helped identify most of the gang.

Arrests followed fast. In nineteen sixty four, the main robbers were sentenced to thirty years in prison. That shocked many people at the time. It was longer than the sentences given for some murders.

vis.label: the sentence given to the main robbers

beats.say: Part five. The escapes.

Then came the escapes. In August nineteen sixty four, Charlie Wilson was broken out of Winson Green prison in Birmingham. In July nineteen sixty five, Ronnie Biggs escaped from Wandsworth prison over the wall.

events: Charlie Wilson broken out of prison

beats.say: Biggs became the most famous of them all. He lived abroad for decades, much of it in Brazil, taunting British authorities. In two thousand and one, old and ill, he came back to Britain voluntarily and was sent back to prison.
Part six. Where did the money go?
Most of the two point six million pounds was never recovered. The notes were used, and only a small number had their serial numbers recorded, so the cash was very hard to trace.

vis.text: Most of the money was never found.

beats.say: And for many of the robbers, it didn't buy a happy ending. Much of it went on lawyers, hiding, and people who helped them, or took a cut for keeping quiet. Several spent most of their remaining lives either in prison or looking over their shoulders.

The Great Train Robbery is often told as a cheeky British caper. But it began with a man being hit over the head in the dark, and ended with long sentences and lives spent running. The money disappeared. The consequences didn't.
